balances.name: Mass and energy balances
balances.description: Check mass balances with recycle, purge and bypass streams, conversion, yield and selectivity, sensible heat, latent heat and heat of reaction, and adiabatic flame temperature with three-choice questions. Many of the calculation questions can be solved with just a calculator.
balances.intro:
Chemical engineering calculations begin with the balance equation: input − output + generation − consumption = accumulation. At steady state the accumulation is zero, and total mass and the amount of each element are conserved even when reactions occur. When using conversion, yield and selectivity, it is important to state clearly which component and which stream each one is based on.
In an energy balance, sensible heat from temperature changes, latent heat from phase changes and the heat of reaction are kept separate and added together. Recycle makes effective use of feedstock in reactions with a low single-pass conversion, and is combined with a purge that prevents inerts from building up. In combustion calculations, the key point is the relationship between percent excess air and adiabatic flame temperature.
balances.blurb: Balance equations, conversion, heat of reaction

thermo.name: Chemical engineering thermodynamics
thermo.description: Check ideal gases and the compressibility factor Z, the van der Waals equation, Raoult's law and relative volatility, the Antoine equation, Henry's law, and equilibrium constants and Gibbs energy with three-choice questions. The calculation questions can be solved with a calculator.
thermo.intro:
Real gases approach ideal-gas behavior at high temperature and low pressure, and the deviation from it is expressed with the compressibility factor Z or the van der Waals equation. In vapor–liquid equilibrium, Raoult's law sets the partial pressure of each component in an ideal solution, and the vapor pressure of each pure component is found from temperature with the Antoine equation. Relative volatility is a measure of how easily a mixture can be separated by distillation.
Chemical equilibrium is linked by ΔG° = −RT lnK; if ΔG° is negative, K is greater than 1. The equilibrium constant is a function of temperature only and follows the van 't Hoff equation, becoming smaller at higher temperatures for exothermic reactions. Pressure and composition shift the equilibrium composition without changing the equilibrium constant, so it is important to keep the two ideas apart.
thermo.blurb: Equations of state, VLE, chemical equilibrium

fluid.name: Fluid flow
fluid.description: Check the continuity equation and the Bernoulli equation, the Reynolds number and laminar versus turbulent flow, the Hagen–Poiseuille equation, pressure drop from the Darcy–Weisbach equation, and pump power, head, NPSH and cavitation with three-choice questions.
fluid.intro:
Flow calculations rest on the continuity equation, which expresses conservation of mass, and the Bernoulli equation, which expresses conservation of energy. The flow regime is judged by the Reynolds number Re = ρuD/μ; in a circular pipe, flow is laminar below about 2300. The laminar pressure drop is given by the Hagen–Poiseuille equation and is proportional to velocity and viscosity.
Piping losses are expressed by the Darcy–Weisbach equation, hL = f(L/D)(u²/2g), where the friction factor f is 64/Re in laminar flow and depends on the Reynolds number and pipe roughness in turbulent flow. Pump power is found from the head and flow rate, and on the suction side enough net positive suction head (NPSH) must be secured to prevent cavitation.

heat.name: Heat transfer
heat.description: Check Fourier's law and the thermal resistance of composite walls, convective heat transfer and the overall heat transfer coefficient, the Nusselt and Prandtl numbers, Stefan–Boltzmann radiation, and the log mean temperature difference of heat exchangers in countercurrent and cocurrent flow with three-choice questions.
heat.intro:
Heat is transferred in three ways: conduction, convection and radiation. Conduction is described by Fourier's law, and a composite wall can be treated as thermal resistances in series. Convection is expressed with a heat transfer coefficient, found from correlations of the Nusselt number with the Reynolds and Prandtl numbers. Radiation is proportional to the fourth power of absolute temperature and becomes more important at higher temperatures.
In heat exchanger design, the heat duty is set by heat balances on both fluids, and the heat transfer area is found from Q = UAΔTlm. The overall heat transfer coefficient U is the reciprocal of the sum of the film resistances on both sides and the wall and fouling resistances, and the largest resistance controls. Countercurrent flow gives a larger log mean temperature difference than cocurrent flow and also allows a temperature cross.

mass-separation.name: Mass transfer and separations
mass-separation.description: Check Fick's law and diffusivities, gas absorption and operating lines, the McCabe–Thiele method for distillation, the minimum reflux ratio and the Fenske equation, liquid–liquid extraction, and membrane separations such as reverse osmosis with three-choice questions. The calculation questions can be solved with a calculator.
mass-separation.intro:
Separation processes exploit differences in component concentration between phases, such as gas and liquid or two liquids. Mass transfer is described by Fick's law with the concentration gradient as the driving force, and diffusivities differ greatly: about 10⁻⁵ m²/s in gases and about 10⁻⁹ m²/s in liquids. In gas absorption, the gap between the operating line and the equilibrium line is the driving force.
In distillation, the McCabe–Thiele method finds the number of theoretical stages by stepping off stages between the equilibrium and operating lines. A larger reflux ratio reduces the number of stages but increases the heat duty, and the minimum reflux ratio and the minimum number of stages at total reflux (the Fenske equation) are the two limits of design. Extraction is organized around the distribution coefficient, and membrane separation around permeation selectivity and driving force.

reactor.name: Reaction kinetics and reactor design
reactor.description: Check reaction order and rate laws, the Arrhenius equation, half-lives, design equations and space time for batch reactors, CSTRs and PFRs, selectivity in series and parallel reactions, catalysts and pore diffusion, and rate-limiting steps in CVD with three-choice questions.
reactor.intro:
Reaction rate depends on concentration and temperature, and the effect of temperature is expressed by the Arrhenius equation. The half-life of a first-order reaction does not depend on the initial concentration, whereas that of a second-order reaction is inversely proportional to it. In reactor design, the required reaction time or volume is found from the design equations of the batch reactor, the continuous stirred-tank reactor (CSTR) and the plug flow reactor (PFR).
For reactions of positive order, a PFR needs a smaller volume than a CSTR for the same conversion. When several reactions occur at once, the selectivity to the desired product changes with temperature, concentration and reactor type. A catalyst speeds up a reaction by lowering the activation energy, but it does not change the equilibrium.

control.name: Process control
control.description: Check the Laplace transform and transfer functions, first-order time constants and step responses, dead time, the damping ratio of second-order systems, the individual actions of PID control, closed-loop stability and cascade control with three-choice questions.
control.intro:
Process dynamics are expressed with transfer functions obtained by the Laplace transform. Many units can be approximated as a first-order lag K/(τs + 1), whose step response reaches 63.2% of the final change at the time constant τ and about 95% at 3τ. Dead time, such as transport delay in piping, is a typical element that lags the phase and makes control difficult.
The core of feedback control is PID control. Proportional action makes a correction proportional to the error but leaves an offset, integral action removes that offset, and derivative action anticipates changes and damps them. Too high a gain causes oscillation and instability, so the condition for stability is that all closed-loop poles lie in the left half-plane.

design-safety.name: Process design and safety
design-safety.description: Check the roles of PFDs and P&IDs and instrument symbols, sizing such as pipe diameters, scale-up, HAZOP, safety valves and rupture disks, flammability limits and Le Chatelier's rule, nitrogen purging, and depreciation and payback period with three-choice questions.
design-safety.intro:
Plant design starts with the PFD, which shows the mass and heat balances, and the details are fixed in the P&ID, which shows the piping, valves and instruments. Equipment is sized from rules of thumb for velocity and residence time. In scale-up, the heat transfer area per unit volume becomes smaller, so heat removal and mixing do not stay the same as in small equipment.
On the safety side, HAZOP identifies deviations from the design intent, and independent protection layers such as safety instrumented systems, safety valves and rupture disks stop an incident from escalating. Flammable gases are basically handled outside their flammable range, and the lower limit of a gas mixture is estimated with Le Chatelier's rule. Investment decisions use economic evaluations such as depreciation and payback period.

particle.name: Particle technology and mechanical operations
particle.description: Check particle size distributions and specific surface area, terminal settling velocity and Stokes' law, constant-pressure filtration with the Ruth equation, centrifugal effect and cyclones, empirical laws of size reduction, and the pressure drop of fluidized beds with three-choice questions. The calculation questions can be solved with a calculator.
particle.intro:
The properties of a powder change greatly with particle size and its distribution. The median diameter differs depending on whether the distribution is number-based or mass-based, and the specific surface area is inversely proportional to particle size. The motion of a particle in a fluid is set by the balance of gravity and buoyancy against drag, and at low particle Reynolds numbers the terminal settling velocity follows Stokes' law and is proportional to the square of the particle diameter.
Filtration, in which resistance increases as the cake builds up, is described by the Ruth equation; in constant-pressure filtration, the square of the filtrate volume is nearly proportional to time. Centrifuges and cyclones speed up settling with centrifugal force and separate finer particles. The energy for size reduction is estimated with the empirical laws of Rittinger, Kick and Bond, and in a fluidized bed the pressure drop across the bed equals the apparent weight of the particles.
particle.blurb: Settling, filtration, size reduction, fluidized beds

adsorption-drying.name: Adsorption, drying and crystallization
adsorption-drying.description: Check the Langmuir and Freundlich adsorption isotherms, batch adsorption balances and breakthrough curves, absolute humidity and wet-bulb temperature, constant-rate and falling-rate drying periods, solubility and supersaturation, and cooling and evaporative crystallization with three-choice questions.
adsorption-drying.intro:
Adsorption is a separation process that collects components from a fluid onto a solid surface. The equilibrium is expressed by an adsorption isotherm; the Langmuir equation, which assumes a monolayer, and the empirical Freundlich equation are widely used. In fixed-bed adsorption, the outlet concentration begins to rise when the mass transfer zone reaches the outlet, and this course is shown by the breakthrough curve. Physical adsorption is exothermic, so the adsorbent can be regenerated by heating or reducing the pressure.
In drying, the state of humid air is expressed by absolute humidity, relative humidity and wet-bulb temperature. The drying rate divides into the constant-rate period, in which the surface is wet and the rate is set by external heat transfer, and the falling-rate period, in which it is set by internal moisture movement. Crystallization uses supersaturation as its driving force and grows crystals in the metastable zone. Supersaturation is created by cooling for substances whose solubility changes strongly with temperature, and by evaporation for those whose solubility changes little.

extraction-absorption.name: Extraction, gas absorption and humidification
extraction-absorption.description: Check the fraction extracted in single and multiple batch extractions, triangular diagrams and tie lines, the two-film theory of gas absorption and overall mass transfer coefficients, packed height from HTU and NTU, flooding in packed towers, and cooling towers and humidification with three-choice questions.
extraction-absorption.intro:
In liquid–liquid extraction, the extraction factor, the product of the distribution coefficient K and the ratio of solvent to feed, sets the fraction extracted. With the same amount of solvent, dividing it into several portions recovers more. Systems in which the feed solvent and the extraction solvent are partially miscible are represented on a triangular diagram; the mixing point is found by the lever rule, and the two phases in equilibrium are found from tie lines.
The rate of gas absorption is treated with the two-film theory, adding the gas-side and liquid-side resistances in series to get the overall mass transfer coefficient. The height of a packed tower is the product of the height of a transfer unit (HTU) and the number of transfer units (NTU), and the gas velocity is kept well below flooding. A cooling tower is a humidification operation that cools water by evaporating part of it, and the outlet water temperature cannot fall below the wet-bulb temperature.

economics.name: Process economics and scale-up
economics.description: Check the six-tenths rule for equipment cost and correction with cost indexes, preliminary estimates, present value and net present value, internal rate of return, payback period, fixed and variable costs, break-even point, and similarity rules for scaling up stirred tanks with three-choice questions.
economics.intro:
Equipment cost does not rise in proportion to size but as a power of capacity, as in the six-tenths rule, so larger plants cost less per unit of capacity. Data from different years are corrected by the ratio of cost indexes, and a preliminary estimate multiplies the corrections for size and time. Investment decisions use net present value, which converts future cash income to present value at a discount rate, and the internal rate of return, with the payback period as a supplementary measure.
Manufacturing cost is split into variable costs, such as raw materials and utilities that are proportional to production, and fixed costs such as depreciation. In scale-up, not every condition can be kept the same as in the small unit. For stirred tanks, a similarity rule suited to the purpose is chosen, such as constant power per unit volume or constant impeller tip speed, and the change in the quantities that cannot be kept constant is estimated.

bioprocess.name: Biochemical engineering
bioprocess.description: Check the Michaelis–Menten equation and the Lineweaver–Burk plot, the Monod equation and specific growth rate, doubling time, batch, fed-batch and continuous culture, dilution rate and washout, yield coefficients, the volumetric oxygen transfer coefficient kLa, and the D value in sterilization with three-choice questions.
bioprocess.intro:
The rate of an enzyme reaction is expressed by the Michaelis–Menten equation, which approaches first order when the substrate concentration is well below Km and zero order when it is well above. Km and the maximum rate can be found from the slope and intercept of the reciprocal Lineweaver–Burk plot. For microbial growth, the Monod equation links the specific growth rate μ to substrate concentration, and the doubling time in the exponential phase is ln2/μ.
Cultures are run in batch, fed-batch or continuous mode; in a chemostat at steady state, μ equals the dilution rate D. If D exceeds the upper limit of growth, the cells are washed out (washout). In aerobic culture, the oxygen supply kLa(C* − CL) easily becomes the limiting factor, and sterilization of the medium is designed with the D value and first-order kinetics of thermal death.

environmental.name: Environmental process engineering
environmental.description: Check the activated sludge process and BOD and COD, SRT and the F/M ratio, coagulation and sedimentation, membrane bioreactors, flue gas desulfurization and denitrification by selective catalytic reduction (SCR), the collection efficiency of dust collectors, and the ideas behind life cycle assessment with three-choice questions.
environmental.intro:
The amount of organic matter in wastewater is expressed as BOD, measured by the oxygen consumed by microorganisms, or COD, measured with a chemical oxidant. The activated sludge process breaks down organic matter with microbial flocs and returns the sludge separated in a clarifier to keep the microbial concentration up; the F/M ratio and the solids retention time (SRT) are central to its operation. Fine turbidity is settled by neutralizing its charge with a coagulant, and a membrane bioreactor separates solids from liquid with membranes instead of a clarifier.
For flue gas, typical methods are desulfurization, which recovers SO₂ as gypsum using limestone, and SCR, which reduces NO to nitrogen with ammonia. The performance of a dust collector is expressed by its collection efficiency, and for units in series the penetrations are multiplied. To compare environmental burdens, LCA evaluates a product's entire life with the functional unit and system boundary aligned.
environmental.blurb: Wastewater, flue gas, dust collection, LCA

electrochem-eng.name: Electrochemical engineering
electrochem-eng.description: Check Faraday's law and current efficiency, the breakdown of cell voltage (theoretical decomposition voltage, overpotential and ohmic loss), specific energy consumption calculations, chlor-alkali electrolysis by the ion-exchange membrane process, alkaline and PEM water electrolysis, limiting current, and the efficiency of batteries and fuel cells with three-choice questions.
electrochem-eng.intro:
By Faraday's law, the amount of substance produced in electrolysis is proportional to the charge passed, and a z-electron reaction needs a charge of zF per mole. In practice part of the charge is lost to side reactions and back reactions, and the fraction that is used is expressed as the current efficiency. The cell voltage is the thermodynamically determined theoretical decomposition voltage plus the overpotentials at both electrodes and the ohmic losses in the electrolyte and separator, and it rises with current density.
Specific energy consumption is the electrical energy per unit of product; it is proportional to the cell voltage and inversely proportional to the current efficiency. In chlor-alkali electrolysis the ion-exchange membrane process, in which a cation-exchange membrane selectively passes Na⁺, is the main method, and water electrolysis comes in alkaline and polymer electrolyte membrane (PEM) types. The upper limit on current density is the limiting current set by mass transfer to the electrode, and the efficiency of batteries and fuel cells is considered in terms of both voltage losses and charge losses.
electrochem-eng.blurb: Cell voltage, energy consumption, water electrolysis

membrane.name: Membrane separation engineering
membrane.description: Check the separation ranges of MF, UF, NF and RO and molecular weight cut-off, permeate flux and transmembrane pressure, the resistance-in-series model, concentration polarization and the film model, rejection, recovery and concentration factor, fouling and backwashing, separation factors of gas separation membranes, and pervaporation with three-choice questions.
membrane.intro:
Membrane separation divides components by differences in pore size or in how readily they dissolve in the membrane; the smaller the species to be separated, the denser the membrane and the higher the pressure used, in the order MF, UF, NF, RO. Performance is expressed by the transmembrane pressure, the driving force that pushes liquid through the membrane, the permeate flux per unit area, and the rejection, which shows how much solute is held back; the flux is inversely proportional to the sum of the membrane and cake resistances.
Concentration polarization, in which rejected solute builds up at the membrane surface, is estimated with the film model Cm/Cb = exp(J/k) and suppressed by raising the cross-flow velocity. With continued operation the flux falls through fouling by deposition and adsorption, and it is recovered by backwashing and chemical cleaning. In gas separation membranes, the permeability and separation factor are set by the solution–diffusion mechanism, and pervaporation, which keeps the permeate side under vacuum, is used to separate azeotropic mixtures.

combustion.name: Combustion and fuels
combustion.description: Check air ratio and theoretical air, higher and lower heating values, flue gas volume and composition, flue gas loss and air preheating, premixed and diffusion combustion, flashback, the Wobbe index, thermal NOx, and SO₂ and the acid dew point with three-choice questions. The calculation questions can be solved with a calculator.
combustion.intro:
Combustion calculations begin by finding, from the fuel composition, the theoretical oxygen and theoretical air needed for complete combustion. Real equipment supplies somewhat more air than theoretical to make up for uneven mixing of fuel and air, and that proportion is expressed as the air ratio m. Heating values come as the higher heating value, which counts the water formed as liquid, and the lower heating value, which counts it as vapor; the difference is the latent heat of vaporization of the water.
The flue gas volume and composition change with the air ratio, and the air ratio can be estimated from the O₂ or CO₂ concentration in the dry flue gas. The sensible heat carried off by the flue gas is the largest loss, so the air ratio is kept appropriate and heat is recovered with air preheaters and similar equipment. On the other hand, hot flames increase thermal NOx, and sulfur in the fuel leads to SO₂ emissions and low-temperature corrosion at the acid dew point, so balancing efficiency against environmental protection and equipment integrity is the key to design.
combustion.blurb: Air ratio, heating value, flue gas

refrigeration.name: Refrigeration, air conditioning and heat pumps
refrigeration.description: Check the components of the vapor-compression refrigeration cycle and the enthalpy at each point, the reverse Carnot cycle and the coefficient of performance, the relation between cooling and heating COP, superheat, absorption refrigerators, CO₂ refrigerant, and the specific enthalpy, mixing and sensible heat factor of moist air with three-choice questions.
refrigeration.intro:
Refrigerators and heat pumps are devices that use work to pump heat from a cold side to a hot side. In the vapor-compression type, the refrigerant evaporates in the evaporator by taking up heat, is raised to high pressure by the compressor, rejects heat in the condenser and returns to liquid, and is depressurized in the expansion valve. Performance is expressed by the coefficient of performance (COP), whose upper limit is TL/(TH − TL) of the reverse Carnot cycle; it is larger the smaller the difference between the evaporating and condensing temperatures.
In air conditioning, the state of moist air is expressed by its dry-bulb temperature, absolute humidity and specific enthalpy, and heating, cooling, mixing and dehumidification are traced on the psychrometric chart. The load on a cooling coil divides into sensible heat, which lowers the temperature, and latent heat of dehumidification, and the sensible fraction is called the sensible heat factor. Refrigerants are required to have little effect on the ozone layer and on global warming, and natural refrigerants such as CO₂ and ammonia, as well as heat-driven absorption machines, are also used.

evaporation.name: Evaporation and multiple-effect evaporators
evaporation.description: Check the mass and energy balances of evaporators, boiling-point elevation and Dühring's rule, the effective temperature difference, steam economy, feed arrangements and temperature distribution in multiple-effect evaporators, MVR and thermal vapor recompression, and evaporator types with three-choice questions. The calculation questions can be solved with a calculator.
evaporation.intro:
Evaporation is the operation of concentrating a solution by boiling it and removing the solvent as vapor. In an evaporator, heating steam (live steam) condenses on the heat transfer surface, and its latent heat boils the solution. The amount of concentrate is fixed by the solute balance, and the steam required is found from an energy balance covering the sensible heat of the feed and the latent heat of evaporation. A nonvolatile solute causes boiling-point elevation, which reduces the effective temperature difference to the steam by the same amount.
The amount evaporated per kg of live steam is called the steam economy; it is usually a little below 1 in a single effect. In a multiple-effect evaporator, where the vapor from one body heats the next, the steam economy rises roughly in proportion to the number of effects, but the effects share the overall temperature difference, so the heat transfer area grows, and the number of effects is set by balancing steam cost against equipment cost. MVR, which raises the pressure of the vapor with a compressor, and thermal vapor recompression with a steam ejector are also energy-saving methods that reuse the latent heat over and over.

optimization.name: Degrees-of-freedom analysis and process optimization
optimization.description: Check how to count degrees of freedom from variables and equations, the degrees of freedom of splitters, flash drums and heat exchangers, tear streams and convergence in recycle calculations, sensitivity analysis, local optima, vertices and shadow prices in linear programming, and minimum energy targets by pinch analysis with three-choice questions.
optimization.intro:
Process calculations begin by counting the degrees of freedom: the number of variables minus the number of independent equations. With zero degrees of freedom the solution is unique; with a positive number, more specifications must be added or the remaining variables chosen by optimization; with a negative number the problem is overspecified. When a process with recycle is calculated unit by unit, one stream in the loop is torn and its values are guessed, and the calculation is repeated until the values returning around the loop agree. Sensitivity analysis checks how strongly the results depend on errors in the assumptions.
Optimization is the problem of choosing the variables that maximize or minimize an objective function while satisfying the constraints. In linear programming, where everything is linear, the optimum appears at a vertex of the feasible region, and the increase in the objective when a constraint is relaxed is called the shadow price. For heat recovery, pinch analysis gives the minimum heating and cooling while keeping the minimum approach temperature, and not transferring heat across the pinch is the basis of energy-saving design.

crystallization.name: Crystallization engineering
crystallization.description: Check how supersaturation is expressed, the metastable zone width, primary and secondary nucleation, rate-limiting steps of crystal growth, the ΔL law and seeding, cooling strategies, antisolvent crystallization, the size distribution of MSMPR crystallizers, and polymorphism and Ostwald ripening with three-choice questions.
crystallization.intro:
Crystallization recovers crystals from solution by creating supersaturation, and it determines not only product purity but also the crystal size and its distribution, the crystal shape and the polymorph. The higher the supersaturation, the more steeply nucleation increases, while within the metastable zone mainly existing crystals grow. In industrial equipment, secondary nucleation arising from collisions of crystals with the impeller and walls is the main source of nuclei, and the balance between the number of crystals and the amount deposited sets the final size.
In batch crystallization, crystal size is made uniform through the amount and size of seed crystals and through cooling or antisolvent addition programmed to keep the supersaturation constant. Continuous crystallization can be organized with the MSMPR model, in which the slope and intercept of the semilogarithmic population density distribution give the growth and nucleation rates. Even the same substance can have polymorphs with different crystal structures, solubilities and stabilities, so controlling which form is obtained is essential for products such as pharmaceuticals.

mixing.name: Agitation and mixing
mixing.description: Check the impeller Reynolds number and power number, power from shaft torque, the role of baffles, impeller types and their selection, discharge flow and mixing time, scale-up similarity rules, the just-suspended speed for solid suspension, aerated agitation and flooding, and mixing of pseudoplastic fluids with three-choice questions.
mixing.intro:
Flow in a stirred tank is organized by the impeller Reynolds number Re = ρND²/μ, formed from the impeller diameter D and the rotational speed N. Power can be written with the power number Np as P = NpρN³D⁵; Np is inversely proportional to Re in the laminar regime and nearly constant in the turbulent regime of a baffled tank. Baffles turn swirling flow into axial and radial flow, and impellers are chosen to suit the liquid and the purpose, such as Rushton turbines or propellers for low viscosity and helical ribbon impellers for high viscosity.
The speed of mixing is expressed by the discharge flow and the mixing time, and in the turbulent regime the product of N and the mixing time is nearly constant. On scale-up, power per unit volume, tip speed, mixing time and other quantities cannot all be kept at once, so the similarity rule is chosen to match the quantity that matters for the purpose, such as solid suspension, bubble dispersion, shear or reaction selectivity. Note too that aeration lowers the power, and too much gas causes impeller flooding.
